Push Pull Legs (PPL) Workout Split

Push Pull Legs organises your training into three categories of movement: pushing movements (chest, shoulders, triceps), pulling movements (back, biceps), and leg movements (quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves). In a standard 6-day PPL, each category is trained twice per week — giving you optimal training frequency for muscle growth.

What is Push Pull Legs?

The Push Pull Legs split — PPL for short — is the most widely used intermediate training structure in gym culture. Its logic is simple: every exercise is either a push (you push weight away from you), a pull (you pull weight toward you), or a leg movement. Grouping these movements keeps synergistic muscles working together on the same day and allows adequate recovery before the next session.

PPL is ideal for intermediate trainees who have been training for at least 6 months and can handle 6 training days per week. It is not suitable for true beginners who have not yet mastered the major compound lifts, or for anyone who cannot commit to 6 consistent sessions per week. If you can train only 3 days, run PPL once through rather than twice.

✅ Pros
  • Each muscle group trained twice per week — research suggests this is optimal for hypertrophy.
  • Clear, logical structure — you always know what you are training and why.
  • High weekly volume accumulation — ideal for muscle building.
  • Muscle groups are pre-fatigued from compound lifts when isolation work is added.
  • Widely documented online — enormous community and resources available.
⚠️ Cons
  • Six days per week is a significant time commitment.
  • Not ideal if life gets in the way — missing one day disrupts the pattern.
  • Recovery can be challenging, especially for natural trainees at high intensity.
  • Beginners may find 6 days overwhelming and would benefit from a full body approach first.

Professor Splits Says:

PPL is one of the most popular splits for good reason — it trains each muscle group twice per week with high volume. The 6-day version is demanding, but results are excellent for dedicated intermediate and advanced trainees.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is PPL good for beginners? ▾
PPL is generally not recommended for true beginners. Six days per week is a lot to manage while still learning the basic compound movements. A 3-day full body routine is a better starting point, moving to PPL after 6 months of consistent training.
Can I do PPL on 3 days instead of 6? ▾
Yes — run through Push, Pull, Legs once per week (3-day PPL). Each muscle is trained once per week, which is less optimal for hypertrophy but completely valid for someone who can only train 3 days.
What is the difference between PPL and Bro Split? ▾
In PPL you train each movement pattern twice per week. In a bro split you train each individual muscle group once per week. Research suggests twice-per-week frequency is generally better for muscle growth, giving PPL a theoretical advantage.
Can I build real muscle on PPL? ▾
Absolutely. PPL is the training structure used by countless successful bodybuilders and physique athletes. With consistent progressive overload and adequate nutrition, PPL produces excellent results.
What if I miss a day on PPL? ▾
Simply continue from where you left off. Do not try to squeeze missed sessions into the same week — extra recovery is better than training fatigued.
